title: The earth, a dharamsaal
carry: the earth is a dharamsaal, a home for living rightly
tomorrow: before sunrise, someone on the porch is talking to the birds. who?

segments.voice: Yesterday, water is the father: a gift you don't pour on the ground, and two grandmothers who turned off the hose. The seedlings are still in their tray.
screen: `WATER IS THE FATHER.` → `SEEDLINGS STILL IN THE TRAY.`

segments.voice: Saturday, and the strip of dirt behind Arjan's building has more people in it than it's ever held. Arjan's mom is turning the soil. Mrs. Haddad brought a bucket of coffee grounds and eggshells for compost. Bebe is directing everyone, mostly Harjit. Maya and Simran are setting chili seedlings and mint cuttings into one long bed. Jasleen is in charge of the watering can, and takes the job very seriously. Nobody asked whose garden it is. It's just the ground, and everyone's on their knees in it.
screen: `ONE STRIP OF DIRT.` → `COMPOST, CHILIES, MINT.` → `BEBE DIRECTS. HARJIT DIGS.` → `WHOSE GARDEN? NOBODY ASKS.`

segments.voice: The Japji's last lines finish the family picture: air the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother. Earlier, in its thirty-fourth pauri on Ang 7, the Japji gives the earth another name. In paraphrase: among nights and seasons, air, water and fire, the One set the earth in place as a dharamsaal, a home for living rightly. So the ground isn't just under the practice. It is where the practice happens. A mother feeds you; you plant, compost, and protect what feeds you back. Now look at these two weeks from this garden. Welcome the stranger: a door with no name, then four cups. Friendship first, over bread. Water for both sides, even for Cole. Honor the humble, at a night-shift table. Air is the guru, under an orange sky. Water is the father, at the hose. And before all that, a freshman staring at his shoes at the bus stop. Today he's laughing with his little sister in the dirt. Earth is the mother, and her lap is big enough for everyone kneeling in it.
screen: `EARTH, THE GREAT MOTHER.` · `A DHARAMSAAL: A HOME FOR LIVING RIGHTLY.` · `PLANT, COMPOST, PROTECT.` · `TWO WEEKS, ONE GARDEN.` · then, large: `EARTH IS THE MOTHER.`

segments.voice: If you can, put both palms flat on the ground: soil, grass, a floor, whatever holds you up right now. Feel it take your weight without asking anything back. Stay there for a few slow breaths, then think of one living thing you could plant or tend this season.
Earth is the mother. From the Japji's last lines: the ground that feeds us, the dharamsaal where we live rightly, tended by planting, compost and protection.
Two weeks in one line: the earth is a dharamsaal, a home for living rightly, and everyone fits in the great mother's lap. Fourteen days, from a bus stop to a garden bed.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Japji, which calls the earth the great mother and a dharamsaal, in morning prayer, and some gurdwaras and Sikh families plant trees and gardens as seva.
